analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal protections against harassment based on sex, race, national origin, disability, or age in schools.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee and died there without ever getting a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it easier for students harassed at school or college to sue for damages by replacing stricter court-made rules with a standard closer to what workers get under federal employment law. It would define sex discrimination to include sexual orientation, gender identity, and pregnancy; require schools to disclose religious exemptions from Title IX; mandate biennial climate surveys of K-12 students about sexual violence; require full-time Title IX coordinators and annual training; let the Education Department impose civil fines; and authorize $100 million in grants to help schools comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Students—especially girls, students of color, LGBTQI+ students, students with disabilities, and pregnant and parenting students—would gain stronger legal remedies when schools fail to address harassment. Anyone victimized in federally funded education programs would get clearer access to compensatory damages, including for emotional distress, plus attorney's fees.

how_it_helps.text: Codifies a lower liability standard and an affirmative defense for schools, replacing the Supreme Court's Gebser/Davis rules that the bill says make it 'extraordinarily difficult' for survivors to win damages.

Explicitly allows recovery of compensatory damages including emotional distress, and punitive damages, plus attorney's and expert fees under Title IX, Title VI, Section 504, and the Age Discrimination Act.

Requires every district and college to designate Title IX coordinators free of conflicts of interest, provide written and oral notice of support services upon receiving a harassment report, and offer protections against retaliation or 'false report' punishment.

Requires schools receiving federal funds to administer biennial climate surveys on sexual assault, harassment, and related misconduct and publish results, and directs the Education Department to develop the survey tool.
Requires institutions claiming Title IX religious exemptions to disclose the request letters and scope of the exemption on their websites.
Authorizes $100,000,000 in grants to help school districts and colleges offset the cost of hiring Title IX coordinators and training staff.

analysis.who_pays: School districts, colleges and universities, and other entities receiving federal education funds would face new compliance duties: hiring coordinators, running biennial surveys, publishing data and religious-exemption disclosures, defending lawsuits under an easier-to-meet liability standard, and potentially paying fines levied by the Education Department.
analysis.who_pays_short: Schools and colleges receiving federal funds

drawbacks.text: The bill does not appear to provide new general funding beyond the $100 million coordinator grants to cover the cost of administering biennial climate surveys, expanded data collection, and training across every federally funded school.

Critics of liability reform argue that easing the standard for damages claims could expose schools to more litigation and drive institutions toward defensive practices, a cost an honest supporter of stronger anti-harassment enforcement would have to weigh.
Requiring religious institutions that claim Title IX exemptions to publish detailed disclosure letters and lists would draw new administrative costs and controversy for those schools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students facing harassment, the bill offers real, concrete gains: a workable path to damages, guaranteed support services, and public data about which schools are failing. The costs fall mainly on institutions as compliance and litigation exposure, with $100 million in grants to offset part of the burden. This is a genuine transfer of leverage from institutions toward students, though its scope across all federally funded schools makes it a large mandate for systems already stretched for resources.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on December 1, 2022, and never advanced before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey (D-PA) introduced the bill on December 1, 2022, with four cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
It was a late-session introduction, filed about a month before the Congress adjourned, giving the committee essentially no window to act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill died without a vote in a Congress that ended weeks after introduction, so the status quo of Title IX enforcement and the existing court-imposed damages standards remain unchanged. Schools, colleges, and religious institutions that would have faced new compliance duties and lawsuits under its liability standard are spared those changes for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Schools and colleges that would face new duties

for.name: Sens. Hirono, Booker, Whitehouse, and Baldwin

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 4 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support listed in the record; no votes were taken and no opposition was formally recorded.

industries.industry: School districts and public K-12 systems
industries.note: The bill would impose hiring, survey, training, and disclosure duties on districts receiving federal funds, while providing $100 million in grants to offset coordinator costs. Its interest in avoiding liability exposure runs against students seeking stronger remedies.

Higher education institutions would face a new private right of action with emotional-distress and punitive damages plus attorney's fees, in exchange for new reporting and enforcement duties. Their interest in limiting legal exposure conflicts with the students the bill aims to protect.
The bill would require these schools to publish their Title IX religious exemption requests and scope on their websites and on the Education Department's site, ending quiet reliance on the exemption.
